parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
parts.passage:
The Rise of Repair Cafés

For many years, people have become accustomed to replacing broken household items rather than repairing them. Whether it is a toaster that no longer works or a chair with a damaged leg, buying a replacement often seems quicker and easier. However, a growing movement known as the repair café is encouraging people to think differently.

Repair cafés are community events where volunteers help visitors fix everyday items free of charge. The idea started in Europe and has spread to many countries around the world. Visitors bring items such as lamps, bicycles, clothing and small electrical devices. Experienced volunteers then work alongside owners to identify problems and attempt repairs.

One reason for the popularity of repair cafés is financial. Replacing products can be expensive, especially during periods of economic uncertainty. By repairing an item instead, people can save money while extending the life of their possessions. Many visitors are surprised to discover that a problem they assumed was serious can often be solved quickly.

Environmental concerns also play an important role. Modern society produces vast quantities of waste every year, and electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing categories. Repair cafés encourage reuse rather than disposal, helping reduce the number of items that end up in landfill sites.

Supporters argue that repair cafés offer benefits beyond saving money and reducing waste. They provide opportunities for people to learn practical skills and meet others in their community. Younger visitors can gain confidence by working alongside experienced volunteers, while older participants enjoy sharing knowledge acquired over many years.

Of course, not everything can be repaired. Some products are designed in ways that make repairs extremely difficult. Manufacturers sometimes use specialised components that are unavailable to the public. Despite these challenges, repair café organisers remain optimistic about the future and believe the movement will continue to grow.
